See the File API specification for more details. metadata.yaml A file used by the data pipeline to describe available data files, listing their associated metadata. See the File API specification for more details. access.yaml A file (potentially with a different name) generated by the data pipeline API to record file access. See the File API specification for more details. Metadata# data_product Identifies which kind of quantity a datum represents (e.g. “human/mixing-matrix”). Path-formatted to permit structure in the filename scheme (defined below). The desired data_product is typically specified in model code, and it is a core part of the data identifiers used in config.yaml, metadata.yaml, and access.yaml. version A semver identifying a version of a data_product (the file API will select the most recent version if this is not specified). component Identifies a part of a data_product. filename Specifies the path to a file, typically relative to the data root. Only required on read, and typically inferred from metadata.yaml. extension Specifies the extension of a file. Required on write to generate a standard filename. Typically provided by a datatype API. run_id Specifies a unique identifier for a model run. Required on write to generate a standard filename, typically generated by the file API. verified_hash Specifies a “verified good” SHA1 hash for a file. Used by the file API to verify file contents. Typically defined in metadata.yaml. calculated_hash Specifies the SHA1 hash computed by the file API for a file. Typically only defined in access.yaml. max_warning Specifies the maximum known warning level for a particular datum. Could be used by the file API to filter “bad” data (currently not supported). Typically defined in metadata.yaml. Filenames# {data root}/{data_product}…/{run_id}.{extension}
e.g. {data root}/human/mixing-matrix/12345.h5

22.title: CLI Examples
22.content:
CLI Examples# This page gives a full working example of a user-written config.yaml file, describes the working config.yaml that fair run generates from it, and shows submission scripts that use it. Note that the language APIs take the working config file as their input, not the user-written one.
The example is the SEIRS epidemiological model used by the simple model repositories (Python, R, Julia, Java, C++, FORTRAN). It registers a file of model parameters from outside the pipeline, runs the model, and records the parameters, the model results and a plot in the pipeline.
From the root of the git repository holding the model, run:
fair init fair pull config.yaml fair run config.yaml and, to share the results on a remote registry:
fair status fair add <namespace>:SEIRS_model/results/model_output/python@v0.0.1 fair push User-written config.yaml# run_metadata: description: SEIRS Model python default_input_namespace: PSU script: python simpleModel/ext/SEIRSModelRun.py register: - namespace: PSU full_name: Pennsylvania State University website: https://ror.org/04p491231 - external_object: SEIRS_model/parameters namespace_name: PSU root: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ path: FAIRDataPipeline/pySimpleModel/main/simpleModel/ext/static_params_SEIRS.csv title: Static parameters of the model description: Static parameters of the model identifier: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-020-0856-2 file_type: csv release_date: 2021-09-20T12:00 version: "1.0.0" primary: false write: - data_product: SEIRS_model/results/model_output/python description: SEIRS model results file_type: csv - data_product: SEIRS_model/results/figure/python description: SEIRS output plot file_type: png run_metadata:# script: the commands to run, or script_path: the path of a script to run. shell: chooses the program that runs it (see Choosing a shell). default_input_namespace: and default_output_namespace: the namespaces used for entries that do not give one. description: a description of the code run. public: whether outputs are public (default true). The local repository, the registry URLs (local_data_registry_url, remote_data_registry_url), the data store (write_data_store) and any namespace not given here are filled in from the CLI’s configuration, set by fair init, so they are usually left out. register:# Data from outside the pipeline, which fair pull downloads and registers.
A namespace: entry registers a namespace (full_name: and optionally website:). An external_object: entry needs namespace_name:, root: and path: (the file’s URL is root followed by path), title:, file_type:, release_date:, version: and primary: (whether this is a primary source), and either identifier: (e.g. a DOI) or both unique_name: and alternate_identifier_type:. description: is optional. Write version in quotes, so that YAML reads it as text. read:# Data products already in the registry that the run reads, given by data_product: and optionally a use: section with version: and namespace:. Objects listed in register: are added to read: by fair run, so they do not need to be listed here.
write:# Data products that the run writes. Each entry needs data_product: and file_type:, and may give description:, public: and a use: section. A use: data_product: lets the script refer to an output by a short name while it is registered under a longer one, as the Julia example does:
write: - data_product: model_output description: SEIRS model results file_type: csv use: data_product: SEIRS_model/results/model_output/julia Versions can be given with template variables, e.g. version: 0.${{DATE}}.0. Without a version, a new data product is written as 0.0.1, and each later run increments the patch number.
Working config.yaml# fair run validates the user-written config, then writes the working config.yaml and the submission script to a new folder in the data store (<data_store>/coderun/<date>T<time>/), and runs the script with FDP_CONFIG_DIR set to that folder. In the working config:
run_metadata: is completed with the local repository (local_repo), its latest commit (latest_commit), its remote URL (remote_repo), the registry URLs, the data store, the default namespaces and public each register: entry becomes a read: entry, and register: is removed every read: and write: entry has a use: section giving the data_product, namespace and exact version to use template variables and wildcards are replaced with their values every write: entry has public: set For example, the run_metadata: of the working config for the example above looks like:
run_metadata: description: SEIRS Model python script: python simpleModel/ext/SEIRSModelRun.py default_input_namespace: PSU default_output_namespace: <your namespace> local_repo: /path/to/pySimpleModel latest_commit: <commit hash> remote_repo: https://github.com/FAIRDataPipeline/pySimpleModel local_data_registry_url: http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/ remote_data_registry_url: https://data.fairdatapipeline.org/api/ write_data_store: /home/<user>/.fair/data/ public: true To see the full working config of a run, look in its folder in the data store, or prepare one without running it using fair run --rehearse config.yaml.
Submission scripts# The script reads the location of the working config and submission script from FDP_CONFIG_DIR, and the local registry token from FDP_LOCAL_TOKEN. The submission script is script.sh (script.bat on Windows). Every API follows the same pattern:
initialise reads the working config and opens a code run, registering the config, the submission script and the code repository. link_read returns the path of an input in the local data store, and link_write returns a path to write an output to. Each is recorded against the code run. finalise renames output files with their hash, and records the outputs, any issues raised, and the code run in the local registry. Python# From pySimpleModel, using pyDataPipeline:
import os import platform import data_pipeline_api as pipeline token = os.environ["FDP_LOCAL_TOKEN"] config_dir = os.environ["FDP_CONFIG_DIR"] config = os.path.join(config_dir, "config.yaml") script = os.path.join(config_dir, "script.bat" if platform.system() == "Windows" else "script.sh") handle = pipeline.initialise(token, config, script) initial_parameters = pipeline.link_read(handle, "SEIRS_model/parameters") model_output = pipeline.link_write(handle, "SEIRS_model/results/model_output/python") model_plot = pipeline.link_write(handle, "SEIRS_model/results/figure/python") # ... run the model, reading initial_parameters and writing model_output and model_plot ... pipeline.finalise(token, handle) R# From rSimpleModel, using rDataPipeline:
library(rDataPipeline) conf.dir <- Sys.getenv("FDP_CONFIG_DIR") config <- file.path(conf.dir, "config.yaml") script <- file.path(conf.dir, "script.sh") if (.Platform$OS.type != "unix") { script <- file.path(conf.dir, "script.bat") } handle <- initialise(config, script) params <- read.csv(link_read(handle, "SEIRS_model/parameters")) # ... run the model ... write.csv(results, link_write(handle, "model_output"), row.names = FALSE) finalise(handle) rDataPipeline can also read and write individual parameters in TOML parameter files, with read_estimate(), write_estimate() and similar functions, and raise issues with raise_issue().
Julia# From the DataPipeline.jl example, using DataPipeline.jl. DataPipeline.initialise() finds the working config, script and token from the environment itself:
using DataPipeline using CSV using DataFrames handle = DataPipeline.initialise() path = link_read!(handle, "SEIRS_model/parameters") static_params = CSV.read(path, DataFrames.DataFrame) # ... run the model ... path = link_write!(handle, "model_output") CSV.write(path, results) DataPipeline.finalise(handle) Java, C++ and FORTRAN# See javaSimpleModel and the Java API, cppSimpleModel and the C++ API, and FortranSimpleModel and the FORTRAN API.

23.title: DPAPI examples
23.content:
DPAPI examples# Note that this is a living document and the following is subject to change. This page gives simple examples of the user written config.yaml file alongside the working config file generated by FAIR run. Note that the Data Pipeline API will take the working config file as an input.
Empty code run# User written config.yaml# run_metadata: description: An empty code run local_data_registry_url: https://localhost:8000/api/ remote_data_registry_url: https://data.fairdatapipeline.org/api/ default_input_namespace: soniamitchell default_output_namespace: soniamitchell write_data_store: /Users/SoniaM/datastore/ local_repo: /Users/Soniam/Desktop/git/FAIRDataPipeline/FDP_validation/ script: |- R -f simple_working_examples/empty_script.R ${{CONFIG_DIR}} Working config.yaml# fair run should create a working config.yaml file, which is read by the Data Pipeline API. In this example, the working config.yaml file is pretty much identical to the original config.yaml file, only ${{CONFIG_DIR}} is replaced by the directory in which the working config.yaml file resides.
run_metadata: description: An empty code run local_data_registry_url: https://localhost:8000/api/ remote_data_registry_url: https://data.fairdatapipeline.org/api/ default_input_namespace: soniamitchell default_output_namespace: soniamitchell write_data_store: /Users/SoniaM/datastore/ local_repo: /Users/Soniam/Desktop/git/FAIRDataPipeline/FDP_validation/ script: |- R -f simple_working_examples/empty_script.R /Users/SoniaM/datastore/coderun/20210511-231444/ latest_commit: 221bfe8b52bbfb3b2dbdc23037b7dd94b49aaa70 remote_repo: https://github.com/FAIRDataPipeline/FDP_validation Submission script (R)# library(rDataPipeline) # Initialise Code Run config <- file.path(Sys.getenv("FDP_CONFIG_DIR"), "config.yaml") script <- file.path(Sys.getenv("FDP_CONFIG_DIR"), "script.sh") handle <- initialise(config, script) finalise(handle) Write data product (HDF5)# User written config.yaml# run_metadata: description: Write an array local_data_registry_url: https://localhost:8000/api/ remote_data_registry_url: https://data.fairdatapipeline.org/api/ default_input_namespace: soniamitchell default_output_namespace: soniamitchell write_data_store: /Users/SoniaM/datastore/ local_repo: /Users/Soniam/Desktop/git/FAIRDataPipeline/FDP_validation/ script: |- R -f simple_working_examples/write_array.R ${{CONFIG_DIR}} write: - data_product: test/array description: test array with simple data Working config.yaml# fdp run should create a working config.yaml file, which is read by the Data Pipeline API. In this example, the working config.yaml file is pretty much identical to the original config.yaml file, only ${{CONFIG_DIR}} is replaced by the directory in which the working config.yaml file resides.
run_metadata: description: Write an array local_data_registry_url: https://localhost:8000/api/ remote_data_registry_url: https://data.fairdatapipeline.org/api/ default_input_namespace: soniamitchell default_output_namespace: soniamitchell write_data_store: /Users/SoniaM/datastore/ local_repo: /Users/Soniam/Desktop/git/FAIRDataPipeline/FDP_validation/ script: |- R -f simple_working_examples/write_array.R /Users/SoniaM/datastore/coderun/20210511-231444/ public: true latest_commit: 221bfe8b52bbfb3b2dbdc23037b7dd94b49aaa70 remote_repo: https://github.com/FAIRDataPipeline/FDP_validation write: - data_product: test/array description: test array with simple data use: version: 0.1.0 Note that, although use: is reserved for aliasing in the user-written config, for simplicity the CLI will always write version here.
Note also that by default, the CLI will write public: true to run_metadata:. The user is however free to specify public: false for individual writes.

24.title: Java
24.content:
javaDataPipeline# The javaDataPipeline Java library allows Java modellers to interface with the FAIR Data Pipeline. The current release, 1.0.0-rc3, requires Java 11 or later and is available on Maven Central:
dependencies { implementation 'org.fairdatapipeline:api:1.0.0-rc3' } The code repo is at 1.0.0-rc4, which has the same API but requires Java 21 or later. It is not yet on Maven Central, so to use it, build it from the repo.
The main purpose of interfacing with the FAIR Data Pipeline is the recording of Coderuns: a Coderun is a recorded session of your modelling code, all the inputs used and outputs generated will be recorded and a Provenance Report will be generated.
The basic idea behind the FAIR Data Pipeline and Coderuns is explained on the FAIR CLI page.
What does it implement?# It reads the working config.yaml written by fair run (not to be confused with the user-written config.yaml). It registers a model Coderun session in the FAIR Data Registry, including all the data inputs and outputs of the model, its code repository, its config.yaml, and its submission (startup) script. It allows the Coderun session to raise Issues with Object_components, the code repository, the config file and the submission script, and these Issues are registered in the Data Registry. It allows reading and writing of Data_products holding a whole file in any (’external’) file format. It allows reading and writing of Data_products containing a FAIR Data Pipeline (TOML) parameter file. netCDF files, recommended for structured data, are read and written whole, like any other file (see netCDF). Usage# A useful starting point to get to know the javaDataPipeline is to explore the java Simple Model. This shows example config.yaml files (see also the CLI example), example main(String[] args) code that allows fair run to call your code, and example Coderun() code for reading/writing input/output Data Products.
The links below give a basic introduction to the javaDataPipeline; these should be read in conjunction with the javaDocs which give more precise specification of the java API.

25.title: Modelling APIs
25.content:
API# Every file a model reads or writes through the data pipeline is a data product, and any file format can be one. A model script asks the API for the path of an input with link_read and for a path to write an output to with link_write, then reads or writes the file whole with its own tools. The pipeline records the file, its hash and the code run that used it.
An end-to-end run# The R, Python, Julia, C++, C and FORTRAN APIs share the same four functions, and the Java API has an equivalent for each (see the table below). fair run prepares the code run and then starts the model, whose script uses them as follows:
* The path returned by link_write is a temporary path. The file is moved to the data store when finalise is called.
† Not every implementation can raise issues yet: the R, Python, Julia and Java APIs can, but the C++, C and FORTRAN APIs cannot.
The names differ slightly between languages:

26.title: Provenance Report
26.content:
Provenance Report# To address the use case of tracing reported results back to the evidence behind them, the data registry can produce a provenance report for each data product.
Provenance is the documented history of the processes in a digital object’s lifecycle. The registry’s reports use the PROV Ontology (PROV-O), which describes provenance in terms of:
entities: things, such as data products, external sources, code, configurations and scripts activities: things that happened, here code runs agents: the people and organisations responsible, here authors and the users who ran the code Provenance reports are available for DataProducts through the REST API, at api/prov-report/<id>/ where <id> is the data product’s id, e.g.:
https://data.fairdatapipeline.org/api/prov-report/3/ Each data product’s API record also links to its report in its prov_report field.
Formats# The format is chosen with the format query parameter (e.g. ?format=provn) or the request’s Accept header:
format Description Media type api the report in the registry’s browsable API page (default in a browser) text/html json PROV-JSON application/json json-ld JSON-LD application/ld+json xml PROV-XML text/xml provn PROV-N text/provenance-notation jpg an image of the provenance graph image/jpeg svg an image of the provenance graph, with links image/svg+xml The jpg and svg formats are only offered if Graphviz was installed on the registry’s machine when the registry started.
Query parameters# Parameter Description depth how many levels of code runs to include (default 1): each further level adds the provenance of the previous level’s inputs, and a data product reached by several routes is expanded once attributes False hides the attributes of each element in the images (shown by default) aspect_ratio the ratio of the images’ height to width (default 0.71, A4 landscape) dpi the resolution of the images For example, api/prov-report/3/?format=svg&depth=2&attributes=False.
What a report contains# A report for a data product written by a code run, with depth=1, has this shape (each element with its PROV relationship, and in brackets the role where there is one):
graph LR; DP([Data product]) -- wasGeneratedBy --> CR[Code run] DP -- "wasAttributedTo (dcterms:creator)" --> AU{{Author}} DP -- "specializationOf or wasDerivedFrom" --> EO([External object]) DP -- wasDerivedFrom --> IN([Input data product]) CR -- "used (fair:input_data)" --> IN CR -- "used (fair:software)" --> REPO([Code repository or release]) CR -- "used (fair:model_configuration)" --> CFG([Model configuration]) CR -- "used (fair:submission_script)" --> SS([Submission script]) CR -- "wasStartedBy (fair:code_runner)" --> RU{{User who ran the code}} Entities# Data products (dcat:Dataset): the namespace (fair:namespace), name (dcterms:title) and version (dcat:hasVersion), the location (prov:atLocation) and SHA-1 hash (fair:hash) of the file, its description, file type (dcterms:format), when it was last modified, and any issues raised against it (fair:issue, with the issue’s description, severity and id). External objects (dcat:Dataset): the source a data product was registered from, with its title, version, release date (dcterms:issued), identifier or alternate identifier and type, description and original location. A data product registered from a primary source is a specializationOf the external object; one registered from a supplementary source wasDerivedFrom it. Code repositories: the location of the code and the commit that was run (fair:commit). A code repository that is a CodeRepoRelease is a dcmitype:Software with its name, version and website. Model configurations and submission scripts: the working config.yaml and the script of each code run, with their location, hash, description and file type. A submission script is a dcmitype:Software. The authors of each of these entities are attached with wasAttributedTo, in the role dcterms:creator.
Activities# Code runs (fair:Run): with the run’s description and its start time. A data product wasGeneratedBy the code run that wrote it, and wasDerivedFrom each data product that code run read. Agents# Authors (prov:Person or prov:Organization): with their name (foaf:name) and identifier, such as an ORCID or ROR ID. The user who ran the code: the author linked to the user who recorded the code run, or the user if they have no linked author. A code run wasStartedBy them, in the role fair:code_runner. Labels and issues# Every element has a prov:label naming it, which the images use:
a data product as <namespace>:<name>@<version> an external object or code release as <title> (<version>) a code run as <description> (<date>) an agent by name a model configuration or submission script by its role, and a code repository by its location In the images, elements with issues have their fair:issue attributes highlighted in red.
Prefixes# All activities, agents and entities have a URI, written with a prefix for the registry that holds them: reg for the central registry (https://data.fairdatapipeline.org/) and lreg for any other registry, such as a local registry. Depending on where the report was produced you may see:
reg:api/data_product/1 or
lreg:api/data_product/1 The other prefixes are for the vocabularies used. In PROV-N, for a local registry, these are:
prefix lreg <http://127.0.0.1:8000/> prefix fair <https://data.fairdatapipeline.org/vocab/#> prefix dcat <http://www.w3.org/ns/dcat#> prefix dcmitype <http://purl.org/dc/dcmitype/> prefix dcterms <http://purl.org/dc/terms/> prefix foaf <http://xmlns.com/foaf/spec/#> prefix rdf <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#> The fair terms (such as fair:Run, fair:namespace and fair:code_runner) are defined on the central registry’s vocabulary page, and each registry serves the same list at vocab/.
Examples# These reports were produced by a local registry loaded with the registry’s example data (python manage.py add_example_data), which holds the SEIRS model used in the CLI examples.

and in PROV-N (api/prov-report/1/?format=provn):

27.title: C
27.content:
C API# The C API is part of the C++ API (cppDataPipeline) and is built with it. It is declared in the header fdp/fdp.h, and is also what the FORTRAN API uses to call the C++ library.
Installation# Build and install the C++ library, which includes the C API, as described on the C++ API page.
Usage# The pipeline is accessed through a FdpDataPipeline struct, which is set up by fdp_init and finalised by fdp_finalise. Every function returns an FdpError code, where FDP_ERR_NONE (0) means success.
Function Description fdp_init(&pipeline, config_file_path, script_file_path, token) Initialise the pipeline. Call once, before any other function fdp_link_read(pipeline, data_product, path, path_len) Get the path of an input data product, recording it as an input of the code run fdp_link_write(pipeline, data_product, path, path_len) Get a path to write an output data product to, recording it as an output of the code run fdp_finalise(&pipeline) Record all data products and metadata in the registry, and free the pipeline fdp_set_log_level(level) / fdp_get_log_level() / fdp_log(level, message) Control and write to the log The config file and script are written by fair run to the folder given by the FDP_CONFIG_DIR environment variable (${FDP_CONFIG_DIR}/config.yaml and ${FDP_CONFIG_DIR}/script.sh, or script.bat on Windows), and the local registry token is given in FDP_LOCAL_TOKEN.
#include "fdp/fdp.h" FdpDataPipeline *pipeline; char input_path[512], output_path[512]; fdp_init(&pipeline, config_path, script_path, token); fdp_link_read(pipeline, "SEIRS_model/parameters", input_path, sizeof(input_path)); fdp_link_write(pipeline, "SEIRS_model/results/model_output/c", output_path, sizeof(output_path)); /* ... read input_path and write output_path ... */ fdp_finalise(&pipeline); The log level can also be set with the environment variable FDP_LOG_LEVEL=[TRACE:DEBUG:INFO:WARN:ERROR:CRITICAL:OFF].
Source code# See the cppDataPipeline repository and the package documentation.

28.title: Jargon buster
28.content: Jargon buster# C# config.yaml a file that specifies the metadata used during file lookup (for read, write, and register), used to configure the overall API behaviour. Code run a recorded run of a model or script, along with its code repository and commit, config file, submission script, inputs and outputs D# Data product a file recorded in the pipeline, identified by its namespace, name and version; any file format can be a data product, and the parameters in TOML parameter files can also be read and written individually Data registry a database for recording metadata about data and model outputs; see local registry and remote registry Data store the folder in which the files registered in a registry are kept (by default ~/.fair/data for the local registry) E# Environment variables (FDP_CONFIG_DIR, FDP_LOCAL_TOKEN) set by fair run for the submission script: the folder holding the working config.yaml and submission script, and the local registry’s API token External object data from outside the pipeline, such as a published dataset identified by a DOI, registered with register: in the user-written config.yaml; the data products registered from it record it as their source F# finalise() calculates the hash of the external objects / data products and renames files, check files exist, etc. I# initialise() reads in the config.yaml file, generates a new entry in code_run and returns id, creates new submission_script (and if necessary creates a new code_repo) entry in local registry L# Local registry a data registry running on your own machine, installed and managed by the CLI (fair registry install) link_read() connects code_run to external_object as input and returns path location (see also link_write()) link_write() connects code_run to data_product as output and returns path location (see also link_read()) N# Namespace a way of grouping data products, usually by the person or organisation that produced them R# Remote registry a shared data registry, such as https://data.fairdatapipeline.org, with which a local registry is synchronised using fair pull and fair push read: a field in config.yaml used to specify the reading of an object (a data product or an external object) that belongs to the user (see also write: and register:) register: a field in config.yaml used to specify the registration of an object (usually an external object) that exists elsewhere (see also write: and read:) add_to_register() registers the object(s) listed in register: (in the config.yaml file) W# Working config the config.yaml written by fair run from the user-written one, with variables, wildcards and versions resolved; this is the file the language APIs read write: a field in config.yaml used to specify the writing of an object (a data product or an external object) that belongs to the user (see also register: and read:)

29.title: Notes on synchronisation
29.content:
Notes# These notes are just extracted from Zulip, so are more stream of consciousness than specifications, but they attempt to describe what a command line tool might do that carried out syncing between the local and remote registries, and what else we might want it to do. Given some of the functionality described here is already provided by the download and upload scripts in the data_pipeline_api repo, it probably makes sense for this to be written in python.
There is an alternative to this command line solution, which would be for the Django interface to the local registry to provide the same (or similar) functionality. This would allow the commands to be access through the web interface, or through the REST API and (optionally) also through the native language interfaces. This would not preclude a command line option as well, because it would simply be a wrapper around the REST API.
Distinction between modelling API and backend# Individual languages communicate with the local registry and the local data store, but communicate no further afield. They need to be able to parse the config.yaml file to understand the relationship between the api requests they receive and the requests they need to make of the registry, however.
All of the syncing:
between the remote registry and the local registry to populate the local data store by downloading data from remote data stores to create remote storage locations for local data that is being pushed to the remote registry is handled by an as-yet-unwritten command line tool, which (for the sake of convenience) I have been calling fdp. This will act a little bit like git. I’m currently imagining it will look like:
fdp pull config.yaml will pull all of the registry entries relevant to this config file into the local registry, and download any files that are referred to in read: or register: blocks to the local data store. fdp run config.yaml will run the submission script referred to in the config.yaml fdp commit <some-token> | <path/to/file> will mark a code run or a specific file (and all of its provenance) to be synced back to the remote registry (once we’ve worked out how to refer to code runs in an intuitive way?) fdp push will sync back any committed changes to the remote registry and upload any associated data to the remote data store (but we still haven’t determined how to specify what to store where) Other commands that might be useful:
fdp status report on overall sync status of registry fdp status <some-token> | <path/to/file> report on sync status of a specific thing (e.g. a code run) or a specific file fdp update pull the most recent registry entries (and associated data) for anything in the current registry fdp gc [--files [--all]] maybe to remove anything from the registry that is not in the provenance history of an unsynced file? Add --files to also delete the associated files from the local data store unless they have restricted accessibility. Add --all to also delete the files from the local data store even if they have restricted accessibility. fdp delete [--force] <some-token> or fdp delete [--force] <path/to/file> delete a specific thing (e.g. a code run) or a specific file from the registry and local data store, adding --force if it is unsynced. fdp info <some-token> | <path/to/file> - return metadata or registry information on a specific registry entry or file The fdp code will handle syncing between two registries using two REST APIs, one at each end, which (I think?) is a significantly harder problem, and so is probably best only solved once though!
We can’t see a way of easily allowing the functionality we need without having a local registry. I think the idea is that the local registry is going to be as standalone as possible. At the moment it’s a single command to install it, and a second to start it up, a third to stop it. Ideally fdp might be able to check if it’s running and start it up and stop it on its own I guess, so the only step would be to install it.
In principle the “local” registry could be on a separate computer and exist for multiple users (say inside a safe haven or on HPC), but it would have to have access to the same filesystem as the machine you’re running on otherwise we get back into issues of remote data access again.
Specialising config.yaml files# One thing we haven’t quite resolved is the distinction between the state of the world when we do fdp pull config.yaml, and the state of the world when we do fdp run config.yaml. A few things may have happened:
the local registry may have been garbage collected using fdp gc, and now: stuff is missing that is required by the code run the remote registry may have been updated and: 2. we haven’t checked, so the local registry is out of date 3. we have run another fdp pull other-config.yaml and so some, but possibly not all, of the local registry entries may have been updated the remote registry may be updated during a run (possibly by calling fdp pull other-config.yaml for a different run), and now: 4. queries made later in a run are inconsistent with queries made earlier in a run. Note this has to happen because we want to be able to write then read something just created during a run - this is one of the requirements that necessitates having a local registry The first two of these are probably easy to handle (crash and ignore, respectively!), but the last two are more tricky. Those may (will?) have issues for the reproducibility of the code run, because there may be no way of being able to reproduce the state of the registry at the point at which it was run. I wonder whether fdp run config.yaml should actually generate a fully qualified config.yaml file specifically for that run, that lists the exact version and data product, etc. with no globbing or text replacement left for the API code to worry about?
Alternatively this could happen when we call fdp pull config.yaml to generate config-2353563.yaml, and fdp run config-2353563.yaml could be executed on the fully qualified version of the file…
config-2353563.yaml was just the name for a file generated by fdp from config.yaml which removes all calculations and lookups, so that human/disease/SARS-CoV-2/* becomes a whole series of entries, one for each data product, which specifies namespace, data product and version so you know exactly what the right version was at the point you ran fdp.
If there’s a working version of the config.yaml that will reproducibly generate the right aliases no matter what you subsequently do to the registry, then it makes things much simpler (and because it is what the API code is actually using, we know that it will generate the right aliases).
fdp pull config.yaml uses the original. Maybe fdp run config.yaml creates the new one and starts up the job, or maybe you have a specific fdp generate config.yaml config-working.yaml to generate the working one? The modelling code should never require an internet connection though.
On a related note to above, the specialised config-working.yaml file should have all of the run_metadata defaults explicitly stated so that changing your config won’t change the run…
Going back to the lack of internet connectivity though, generating the working yaml file doesn’t require an internet connection though. It’s just saying “given the current state of the local registry, what does this config.yaml file really mean in practice if I use it?”.
Local data storage# How about this? You setup a new local registry, go to /Users/johnsmith/datastore and run fdp config "johnsmith" to set this directory as your data store. This will generate an API token for the local registry and add an entry to .scrc/.users noting the fact that the johnsmith username / namespace is associated with /Users/johnsmith/datastore… or do something fancier to specify the local registry url, or even set passwords? Your config.yaml now contains a username / namespace rather than a list of defaults associated with your account.
If someone wants to share your datastore, that’s fine, they run fdp config "otherperson" from the same working directory and their details are added to .scrc/.users.
fdp config might also generate a specific login node, recorded in .users?

30.title: RO Crate Objects
30.content:
Research Object Crate (RO-Crate)# A Research Object Crate (RO-Crate) packages research data together with the metadata that describes it, in a single folder or zip file with a machine-readable description, ro-crate-metadata.json. The data registry can produce an RO-Crate for any data product or code run, so that results can be shared or archived together with their provenance: the code that made them, the inputs it read and where those came from.
The crates conform to the Process Run Crate 0.6 profile of the Workflow Run RO-Crate family, which describes how a piece of software was run to produce files.
Getting a crate# Crates are available through the REST API:
Address Crate for api/ro-crate/data-product/<id>/ a data product, and the files that were used to produce it api/ro-crate/code-run/<id>/ a code run: all of its outputs, and the files it used api/ro-crate/?data_product=<id>&data_product=<id> several data products, e.g. outputs of different code runs, together with the provenance of each The API records of each data product and code run link to their crates in their ro_crate field.
Formats# The format is chosen with the format query parameter or the request’s Accept header:
format Description zip the crate as a zip file, holding ro-crate-metadata.json and the files chosen by pack json or json-ld the contents of ro-crate-metadata.json alone, with no files api the metadata in the registry’s browsable API page (default in a browser) For example, to download the crate of data product 3 with two levels of provenance:
https://data.fairdatapipeline.org/api/ro-crate/data-product/3/?format=zip&depth=2 Query parameters# Parameter Description depth how many levels of code runs to include (default 1): each further level adds the code runs that produced the previous level’s inputs, and a data product reached by several routes is added once level what is recorded about every file: 1, its hash and any persistent identifier, with its source’s metadata; 2, also the address the registry’s copy can be downloaded from (contentUrl). The default is 2 for a zip and 1 otherwise pack which files’ contents a zip holds (see below); the default is roots Choosing which files are packed# Every file in the crate’s provenance is described in the metadata, but only some are copied into a zip:
pack Files packed none none roots the data products the crate is for (for a code run’s crate, its outputs) supplements as roots, plus every file registered from a supplementary source: data that was requested or derived from a source, such as an extract made by a data service, which no identifier would return again all every file The working config and submission script of each code run are always packed in a zip. Only public files are packed: a file that is not public is described by the address of its storage location in the registry. Outputs of a code run that are outside the crate’s provenance are described, without contentUrl, and never packed.
Files from primary sources, which can be fetched again by their identifier (such as a DOI), only need to be packed with all. A crate packed with roots therefore stays small while still recording where every input can be found.
Contents of a crate# Layout# Each data product’s file is at <namespace>/<name>/<version>.<extension>, the same layout a registry’s data store uses for the files it pulls, and each code run’s working config and submission script are in model_config/ and submission_script/ under their own file names. Every file has this path in the metadata whether or not it is packed. For example, the crate of the results of the Python SEIRS model (written to the namespace user_4) holds:
ro-crate-metadata.json PSU/ SEIRS_model/ parameters/ 1.0.0.csv user_4/ SEIRS_model/ results/ figure/ python/ 0.0.1.png model_output/ python/ 0.0.1.csv model_config/ config.yaml submission_script/ script.sh Files# Each file is a File entity with:
name and version: the data product’s name and version namespace: a Namespace entity, with the namespace’s name, its full name as alternateName, and its website as url identifier: the uuid of the file’s object in the registry sha1: the SHA-1 hash of the file’s contents encodingFormat: the file’s media type, from its file type description, and contentUrl at level=2 author: the file’s authors issue: any issues raised against the file, each as <uuid> severity <severity>: <description> (issue is one of the registry’s own terms, defined on its vocabulary page) The working config and submission script of each code run are entities of type File and SoftwareSourceCode, with their file name as name and the same identifier, sha1, encodingFormat, description and author properties.
External sources# A data product registered from outside the pipeline (an external_object: in the user config) is a File like any other, and its source is a Dataset entity: its persistent identifier (such as a DOI) as identifier, its title as name, and its version, datePublished, description, alternate identifier and, where the registry recorded where the file was fetched from, contentUrl. There is one source entity per source the registry knows.
A file from a primary source, where the file is the identified item or one of its files, points to the source with sameAs. A file from a supplementary source, where the data was requested or derived from the source, points to it with isBasedOn. The source’s description holds the request, where the registry was given it, so the file can be reproduced. A deposit registered as a whole is a source of its own, and the sources of files under its identifier are isPartOf it. Code runs# Each code run is a CreateAction, as described in Software used to create files, with:
Property Value identifier the code run’s uuid, which is also in its @id (urn:uuid:<uuid>) name, description, startTime code run <uuid>, the code run’s description, and when it was run instrument the code that was run (or the submission script, for a run without a code repository) object the input files, the working config and the submission script model_configuration, submission_script which of those files is the working config and which the submission script result every output of the code run agent the author who ran the code The instrument is a SoftwareApplication identified by the repository’s address and the commit that was run, as <repository>#<commit>, with the repository as its url. For a code release (a CodeRepoRelease), its name and softwareVersion are the release’s name and version; otherwise its name is the repository’s path and its version is the commit.
People and licences# Authors are identified by their ORCID, GitHub account or other identifier where the registry has one, and otherwise by their uuid (as urn:uuid:<uuid>). An author with a ROR id is an Organization, and any other a Person. A user with no linked author is identified by a local id. The licences of the files the crate is for are the crate’s license, identified by their URL, or by the file they apply to where they have none. A crate whose files have no licence is licensed CC BY 4.0. Individual files may carry their own licences. ro-crate-metadata.json itself is made available under the CC0 Public Domain Dedication. The crate’s publisher is FAIR Data Pipeline, and its datePublished is when it was generated. Nothing in a crate is identified by its row number in the registry that produced it.
Example# This is part of the ro-crate-metadata.json of the crate above (api/ro-crate/data-product/7/?format=json-ld), produced by a local registry loaded with the registry’s example data (python manage.py add_example_data). It shows the code run that wrote the results, the code it ran, and the parameters it read, which were registered from a primary source. The root dataset, licences, people and other files, and the files’ encodingFormat, are left out:

31.title: C++
31.content:
cppDataPipeline# The cppDataPipeline library contains functions used to interface with the FAIR Data Pipeline in C++. It also provides the C API.
Building# The library is built using CMake (3.13 or later) and requires a C++11 compatible compiler. It is recommended that you install CURL first.
cmake -Bbuild cmake --build build For multi-config generators such as Visual Studio, Xcode or Ninja Multi-Config, the build type must be set to Release:
cmake --build build --config=Release To install the library system-wide (this requires Boost, or build a shared library with -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON):
cmake --build build --target install It can then be used in other CMake projects:
find_package(fdpapi) target_link_libraries(my_project PRIVATE fdpapi::fdpapi) To build and run the unit tests, configure with -DFDPAPI_BUILD_TESTS=ON and run ./build/bin/fdpapi-tests. The tests need a running local registry (fair registry start).
Usage# The current release is 0.2.7. The library is declared in the header fdp/fdp.hxx, in the namespace FairDataPipeline. A pipeline is created with DataPipeline::construct, which returns a shared pointer, and provides the methods link_read, link_write and finalise:
#include "fdp/fdp.hxx" namespace FDP = FairDataPipeline; // config_path and script_path are in the folder given by FDP_CONFIG_DIR, // and token is the value of FDP_LOCAL_TOKEN FDP::DataPipeline::sptr pipeline = FDP::DataPipeline::construct(config_path, script_path, token); std::string input = "SEIRS_model/parameters"; std::string output = "SEIRS_model/results/model_output/cpp"; std::string input_path = pipeline->link_read(input); std::string output_path = pipeline->link_write(output); // ... read input_path and write output_path ... pipeline->finalise(); The environment variable FDP_LOG_LEVEL=[TRACE:DEBUG:INFO:WARN:ERROR:CRITICAL:OFF] sets the logging level.
See the package documentation for instructions and examples, and the C++ simple model for a complete example.
Source code# See the package’s code repo.

33.title: FORTRAN
33.content:
FortranDataPipeline# The FortranDataPipeline library contains functions used to interface with the FAIR Data Pipeline in Fortran. It depends on the C++ API, which it calls through the C API.
Installation# The library is built using CMake (3.20 or later), and needs a compiler suite that supports C++11 and Fortran 2003. It is recommended that you install CURL first.
cmake -Bbuild cmake --build build To install the library system-wide:
cmake --build build --target install It can then be used in other CMake projects:
find_package(fdpfort) target_link_libraries(my_project PRIVATE fdpfort::fdpfort) Usage# The current release is 0.2.1. The library is the module fairdatapipeline, whose FdpDataPipeline type has the following procedures. Each takes an optional err argument, which is set to FDP_ERR_NONE (0) on success:
Procedure Description pipeline%init(config_file_path, script_file_path, token, err) Initialise the pipeline at the start of a run pipeline%link_read(data_product, err) Return the path of an input data product, recording it as an input pipeline%link_write(data_product, err) Return a path to write an output data product to, recording it as an output pipeline%finalise(err) Record all data products and metadata in the registry at the end of a run The module also provides fdp_log(level, message, err), fdp_set_log_level(level) and fdp_get_log_level() to control and write to the log, with the levels FDP_LOG_TRACE to FDP_LOG_OFF.
use fairdatapipeline, only: FdpDataPipeline type(FdpDataPipeline) :: pipeline character(:), allocatable :: input_path, output_path integer :: err ! config_path and script_path are in the folder given by FDP_CONFIG_DIR, ! and token is the value of FDP_LOCAL_TOKEN call pipeline%init(config_path, script_path, token, err=err) input_path = pipeline%link_read("SEIRS_model/parameters", err=err) output_path = pipeline%link_write("SEIRS_model/results/model_output/fortran", err=err) ! ... read input_path and write output_path ... call pipeline%finalise() The environment variable FDP_LOG_LEVEL=[TRACE:DEBUG:INFO:WARN:ERROR:CRITICAL:OFF] sets the logging level.
See the Fortran simple model for a complete example.
Testing# The tests need a running local registry (fair registry start). Build with -DFDPFORT_BUILD_TESTS=ON and run the run-tests target:
cmake -Bbuild . -DFDPFORT_BUILD_TESTS=ON cmake --build build --target run-tests Source code# See the package’s code repo.

34.title: Uses cases
34.content:
Use Case 1. (Pre-process and) upload a new dataset using script/config file# Actor: A Data Curator wants to upload a dataset to the registry – this will likely involve a pre-processing step to convert a ‘raw dataset’ into a suitable ‘processed dataset’ that can be used by a model. Actor interrogates registry to confirm status of all prerequisite data resources

Output from model uploaded to registry
Model output used in rmd-type framework to generate policy briefing

Status reports for any given model run and for the entire the briefing can be generated (listing dependencies, provenance, flagging up QA status and issues)

Again – what do we do with the data types (like the reports) that are not in a core data format?
Could provenance reports and QA info be generated for any “object” in the registry?

Basic Flow:
Actor collates list of data resources required for model run
Actor interrogates registry to review status of all prerequisite data resources
Where a data resource is flagged as ‘at risk’, or has some other property (too recent? Might want to roll back to an earlier version) actor can request a list, with summary metadata (tbc), of other ‘views/components/distributions’ or versions of that data resource
Actor selects view for use in this run

The actor has been able to make an informed choice of data resource views Questions: Do we want to flag up data status/issues via web interface and also during programmatic access?

Or modeller has an analysis that they have previously done, wants to know if they ran it again are any of the data products or model code updated?
Preconditions: Actor has an account (if required) to access data registry.
Basic Flow:
Actor finds code run or data output to investigate
Actor accesses registry entry for the specified output
Actor queries registry to establish the status of the data resources relative to the current state of the registry
Registry produces list of pre-requisite data resources, and (optionally) the status of these at the time the output was generated (I assume these latter are available from the metadata of the output itself)
Postconditions:
No change to registry
Actor has sufficient information to assess the output to assess whether the data is
Up to date
Is there a newer version of any of the data or model code?
Has any of the existing data now got attached warnings / invalidated
Actor has sufficient information to have an informed discussion with modeller as to the current validity of the past output
Use Case 10. Retrospective assessment of status, when generated, of a pipeline validated output# Actor: Policy broker who has a query about the provenance of an output, previously generated and registered within the pipeline. There is a need to confirm whether the output had appropriate caveats attached when circulated. (Sorry to be negative, but I can see this happening… )
Preconditions: Actor has an account (if required) to access data registry.
Basic Flow:
Actor accesses registry entry for the specified output
Actor queries registry to recover the status of the data resources used at the time the output was generated (I assume these latter are available from the metadata of the output itself; if these are not available, is there sufficient information in the metadata for them to be reconstructed?)
Postconditions:
No change to registry
Actor has sufficient information to assess the output from the point of view of the needs of policy customers
Exception cases:
The obvious one is the situation where the output has not been registered in the registry, but where there is sufficient knowledge of the data resources used to be confident about what was actually used. However, I think we should not seek to cover this scenario, since the users have already broken the system, and the existence of a tool to retrospectively cover everyone’s back might just encourage poor behaviour.. Questions: How would we keep track of history of status/issues to be able to re-create status reports from past points in time? If status consists of timestamped issues and QA reports that are then immutable, then this would be possible.
How important is it that this is easy / convenient vs “possible by digging into the database”?
Use Case 11. Understanding of local data# Actor: Modeller has datasets locally on computer, wants to know if they are already on registry, and if so what they are
Preconditions: Actor has an account (if required) to access data registry.
Basic Flow:
Actor finds file / files to investigate
Actor queries registry to recover the status of the data
Postconditions:
No change to registry
Actor has sufficient information to assess the output to assess whether the data is
In registry at all (from checksum)
Up to date – is there a newer version?
Has attached warnings / invalidated
Exception cases:
What if the data was in the registry but has been corrupted or accidentally edited, is there some way of telling what it (probably?) should have been? Notes: Possible a tool for data import to the registry that calculates checksums could be run over the directory

Actor: Member of public wants to understand provenance of reported results
Basic Flow:
Possible ways this could work:
1. Via a searchable interface to the data registry
2. Have access to PDF (or other format) of policy document
can use PDF directly to identify provenance report to display 2. Have access to pdf of report and can use pdf to identify provenance report to display
PDF has embedded DOI or link to provenance report in registry
PDF is uploaded by user and the system identifies it via a checksum
PDF has a unique title/identifier used to look up provenance report
Notes: Report documents must be (manually?) added to registry for this to work. Or must be part of workflow for latex document creation.
Use Case 13. Actor wants to identify changes between model outputs# Any user of the model outputs (e.g. modeller, policy maker) wants to know what changed between two published model outputs / reports, and generates a diff between the provenances
Basic Flow:
This requires use case 12, plus a mechanism for displaying a comprehensible diff.
Use Case 14. From a screen on the visualisation platform, the user wants to follow a link to a provenance report for the underlying data and processing# Possible ways this could work:
1. visualisation platform itself uses traceability framework within it to generate provenance reports
2. visualisation platform manually links back to provenance of the components that are interactively selected
Use Case 15. Initial quick look at dataset visualisations online# Any user (policy maker, modeller, etc.) may either want to investigate public datasets registered in data registry visually, or may be investigating a provenance reports and want to see what a dataset is that is traced in report.
Basic flow:
Links directly from data pipeline to visualisation infrastructure, no programming
Use Case 16. Actor wants to do a model run inside a safe haven# Preconditions: Actor has an account (if required) to access data registry, actor has access to safe haven, metadata is public
Basic Flow:
Possible ways this could work:
1. Registry sits inside safe haven, as does all data required for analysis – full pipeline runs inside safe haven
Registry must sync with an external registry (at simplest just a read-only copy) or have a direct external public interface to ensure public availability of provenance data, otherwise many use cases will break – especially anything policy- or public-facing, where users will not have access to safe haven 2. Registry sits outside safe haven, public data can be hosted outside safe haven, but is pulled in as required to be used in the modelling run along with the private data. Pipeline run generates log files that are then pushed back to registry after run.
Then as use case 4.

Potential issue with 1 – how does post-processing of results generated in a safe haven (e.g. to produce reports) work if write access to registry is only available inside safe haven?

How this could work:
Local pipeline scripts have to know about local cache of private files, then pipeline can execute as normal in use case 4.

35.title: Coderun
35.content:
javaDataPipeline Coderun# The main class used to interface with the FAIR DataPipeline in Java, is the Coderun class.
Users should initialise the Coderun instance using a try-with-resources block or ensure that .close() is explicitly called upon finishing.
The Coderun constructor needs a Path to the config.yaml, a Path to the script.sh, and the registry authentication token.
The user then would access the input data product(s) using coderun.get_dp_for_read(dataproduct_name) and output data product(s) using coderun.get_dp_for_write(dataproduct_name, extension).
From the resulting data_product we can then access either one unnamed object_component: Object_component_read oc = dp.getComponent() or any number of named object_components: Object_component_read oc1 = dp.getComponent('ComponentName').
Data in the FAIR Data Pipeline’s internal format (TOML parameter files) is written to (or read from) named Object_components, while other file formats (such as CSV or netCDF) are written to (or read from) just 1 unnamed Object_component.
Here is an example of a Coderun writing a CSV file to one unnamed Object_component:
try (var coderun = new Coderun(configPath, scriptPath, token)) { Data_product_write dp = coderun.get_dp_for_write(dataProduct, "csv"); Object_component_write oc = dp.getComponent(); Path p = oc.writeLink(); write_my_csv_data_to_path(p); } And for reading:
try (var coderun = new Coderun(configPath, scriptPath, token)) { Data_product_read dp = coderun.get_dp_for_read(dataProduct); Object_component_read oc = dp.getComponent(); Path p = oc.readLink(); read_my_csv_data_from_path(p); } Here is an example of a coderun writing Samples to one named Object_component:
try (var coderun = new Coderun(configPath, scriptPath)) { ImmutableSamples samples = ImmutableSamples.builder().addSamples(1, 2, 3).rng(rng).build(); String dataProduct = "animal/dodo"; String component1 = "example-samples-dodo1"; Data_product_write dp = coderun.get_dp_for_write(dataProduct, "toml"); Object_component_write oc1 = dp.getComponent(component1); oc1.writeSamples(samples); }

37.title: Issues
37.content:
javaDataPipeline Issues# Issues can be attached to Object_components, as well as to the Submission Script, Config File, and Code Repo.
Issues can be created and then linked to the elements that they apply to, or they can be raised directly on the element it refers to.
Here is an example of the creation then linking of an Issue to components, Script, and Code Repo:
try (Coderun coderun = new Coderun(configPath, scriptPath, token)) { Data_product_read dp = coderun.get_dp_for_read("existing/dpname"); Object_component_read oc1 = dp.getComponent("comp1"); Object_component_read oc2 = dp.getComponent("comp2"); Issue i = coderun.raise_issue("A serious issue", 10); i.add_components(oc1, oc2); i.add_fileObject(coderun.getScript(), coderun.getCode_repo()); } And here is an example of raising an issue directly with a component and a Script:
try (Coderun coderun = new Coderun(configPath, scriptPath, token)) { Data_product_read dp = coderun.get_dp_for_read("existing/dpname"); Object_component_read oc1 = dp.getComponent("comp1"); oc1.raise_issue("A serious issue", 10); coderun.getScript().raise_issue("Another pretty serious issue", 9); }

40.title: Run
40.content:
Running your code# Below is a brief explanation how to make use of the Java FAIRDataPipeline library and actually getting your code to run from the FAIR CLI command line interface. The actual command to run your Java code is given in the script: line in the config.yaml. In my case I run the Java code using gradle run --args "${{CONFIG_DIR}}". You’ll have to change this if you don’t use gradle.
Below is an example config.yaml, stored in your projects /src/main/resources:
run_metadata: default_input_namespace: test description: Java test coderun script: | gradle run --args "${{CONFIG_DIR}}" write: - data_product: test/results/my-result description: test results file_type: csv Your Java code then needs to read the registry token from the environment variable, and create a coderun using the config.yaml and script.sh files that will be placed in the CONFIG_DIR by FAIR CLI:
String token = System.getenv("FDP_LOCAL_TOKEN"); Path configPath = Path.of(args[0]).resolve("config.yaml"); Path scriptPath = Path.of(args[0]).resolve("script.sh"); try(var coderun = new Coderun(configPath, scriptPath, token)) { // create DP, Object_component, write results; } From your project root you can then just run the FAIR CLI commands:
fair init fair pull src/main/resources/config.yaml fair run src/main/resources/config.yaml

41.title: Debug
41.content:
Debugging / troubleshooting# Logger# The javaDataPipeline library uses SLF4J (Simple Logging Facade for Java).
You can either use this with the SLF4J simple logger, or it can bind to your own favourite logging framework. In order to set the default simple logger to more verbose logging:
add the org.slf4j:slf4j-simple dependency set the log level: System.setProperty(org.slf4j.impl.SimpleLogger.DEFAULT_LOG_LEVEL_KEY, "TRACE");
Running manually# Instead of running:
fair run src/main/resources/config.yaml You can call fair run and your actual java code separately:
fair run --ci src/main/resources/config.yaml gradle run --args "/tmp/tmpXXXXXXX/data_store/jobs/<timestamp>" The actual tmp location is shown as output from the fair run command.
This may help debug/troubleshoot.

45.title: Introduction
45.content:
Notice: This Documentation is in the process of being updated, some of the information may be out of date, or incorrect.
Introduction# The FAIR Data Pipeline is intended to enable tracking of provenance of FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable) data used in epidemiological modelling. Pipeline APIs written in C, C++, FORTRAN, Java, Julia, Python and R can be called by modelling software for data ingestion. These interact with a local relational database storing metadata and the local filesystem, and are configured using a yaml file associated with the model run. Local files and metadata can be synchronised with a remote registry via a command line interface (fair).
The key benefits of using the FAIR Data Pipeline are:
Opensource, all code is available on the FAIRDataPipeline GitHub Data recorded in a FAIR fashion (metadata on all data and code open and available for inspection) Provenance tracing allows model outputs to be traced to inputs and modelling code Multiple language support Designed to run on a broad range of platforms (including HPC, inside Safe Havens) Designed to be set up and completed online (to down-/up-load data) and run offline (Safe Havens will require this) Open metadata provides knowledge of or access to shared central data for specific domains (e.g. COVID-19 epidemiological modelling) Running Models# To use the FAIR Data Pipeline with a piece of modelling software, you must add a language specific Pipeline API as a dependency and interact with data registered in the pipeline via the methods it presents. Each model run must be configured using a config.yaml file which specifies inputs and outputs by metadata.
